what: MGIC Investment insures mortgage lenders against borrower default. When an American buys a home with a deposit below twenty per cent, the lender requires private mortgage insurance; MGIC collects a monthly premium and pays the lender if the loan goes bad. It is the oldest company in the industry.
customers: Mortgage lenders and the government-sponsored buyers of mortgages, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which require insurance on high loan-to-value mortgages.
money: Premiums on insurance in force across a large book of American mortgages.
Returns on the invested premium reserves.
moat: Private mortgage insurance is a licensed industry with six main participants, capital requirements set by the government-sponsored enterprises, and pricing driven by proprietary risk models. Insurance written stays in force for years while the borrower pays monthly, so a good underwriting year produces income for a decade, and the reserves earn investment income at no extra cost.
risks: This business loses money precisely when house prices fall, which is when everything else falls too — the risk cannot be diversified away.
The current book was largely written against house prices at historic highs, so the collateral behind it is at its most expensive.
Revenue has been flat at about $1.2B for five years, so growth depends entirely on mortgage origination volumes recovering.
Credit losses have been minimal for over a decade, which means the reported profitability reflects an unusually benign period.
Only six analysts cover the stock, so the $30.17 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Last year’s net margin was 60.8%, and free cash flow of $707.7M on $1.2B of revenue shows how profitable this is when losses are low.
The shares trade at about 8.3 times earnings, 6.6 times EV/EBITDA and 7.5 times free cash flow.
Insurance in force generates premiums for years after it is written, making revenue unusually predictable.
Debt of $646.1M is modest and industry capital requirements are far stricter than before the financial crisis.
Borrowers whose homes have appreciated since purchase are far less likely to default, which improves the existing book.
watch: Delinquency rates on insurance in force. Premiums are predictable and losses are not, so delinquencies are the only forward-looking number in this business.
view: MGIC is the oldest private mortgage insurer in America, which means it has lived through what happens when this business goes wrong. In 2008 the industry’s loss assumptions proved badly inadequate, several competitors failed, and MGIC itself came close. Anyone looking at a 60.8% net margin and an 8.3 times earnings multiple should hold that history in mind, because this is a business that looks wonderful for a decade and then explains itself in eighteen months.

What has genuinely improved is worth stating fairly. Capital requirements set by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are far stricter now, the loans being insured are documented and income-verified in ways 2006 vintages were not, and the risk models are better. The specific failure mode of 2008 — undercapitalised insurers against systematically mispriced risk — has been addressed by regulation rather than merely by good intentions. MGIC carries $646 million of debt, which is modest.

What has not changed is the nature of the exposure. Mortgage insurance loses money when house prices fall, which is also when equities fall, credit spreads widen and unemployment rises. There is no diversification available — it is a single correlated bet on American housing. And the current book was written largely against house prices at historic highs, which means the collateral is at its most expensive. The offsetting point is genuine: borrowers who bought with small deposits several years ago now hold substantial equity from appreciation, and borrowers with equity do not walk away.

Revenue has been flat at about $1.2 billion for five years, so this is not a growth story — it is a very profitable, very cheap, very correlated bet with a buyback. At 8.3 times earnings that is a reasonable proposition provided the holder understands what they own. Delinquency rates on insurance in force move before the earnings do, and a sustained rise there is not something to monitor and discuss; it is the exit signal.
bull: Post-crisis capital rules and verified underwriting hold through any mild downturn, accumulated home equity keeps defaults minimal, and 8.3 times earnings funds large buybacks.
bear: House prices fall against a book written at the peak, delinquencies rise, and a single correlated bet on American housing takes losses across the whole portfolio.
